items.title: The Sixth Doctrine: All Suffering Traces to Past Deeds Alone

items.zh: 宿作因論者，猶如有一，若沙門、若婆羅門，起如是見，立如是論，廣說如經。凡諸世間所有士夫補特伽羅所受者，謂現所受苦。皆由宿作為因者，謂由宿惡為因。由勤精進吐舊業故者，謂由現法極自苦行。
items.en: The doctrine of prior deeds as cause: there are certain renunciants or brahmins who hold such a view and establish such a doctrine, stated in full as in the sūtra. Whatever suffering any person in the world experiences is invariably caused by prior deeds — that is, by past unwholesome karma. Through diligent, strenuous effort, one purges this old karma — that is, through extreme self-mortification practised in this very life.

items.zh: 現在新業由不作因之所害故者，謂諸不善業。如是於後不復有漏者，謂一向是善性故，說後無漏。由無漏故業盡者，謂諸惡業。由業盡故苦盡者，謂宿因所作及現法方便所招苦惱。由苦盡故得證苦邊者，謂證餘生相續苦盡。謂無繫外道作如是計。
items.en: New karma in the present is prevented by the cause of non-action — that is, by refraining from every unwholesome deed. Thereafter, no further contamination arises — since one's nature has become entirely wholesome, no further contamination follows. Because there is no further contamination, karma is exhausted — namely, every unwholesome karma. Because karma is exhausted, suffering is exhausted — namely, the suffering produced both by prior karma and by present ascetic effort. And because suffering is exhausted, one realises the very limit of suffering — that is, one realises the complete cessation of suffering across every future rebirth. It is the Nirgrantha ascetics — the unclothed renunciants — who hold this position.

items.zh: 問：何因緣故，彼諸外道起如是見，立如是論？答：由教及理故。教如前說。理者，猶如有一，為性尋思，為性觀察，廣說如前。
items.en: Question: For what reason do those non-Buddhist teachers hold this view and establish this doctrine? Answer: Because of scripture and reasoning. Scripture is as explained before. Reasoning means that someone is a speculator by nature and an examiner by nature, as explained at length before.

items.title: Why They Believed This: Good People Suffer, Bad People Prosper

items.zh: 由見現法士夫作用不決定故。所以者何？彼見世間雖具正方便，而招於苦；雖具邪方便、而致於樂。彼如是思：若由現法士夫作用為彼因者，彼應顛倒。由彼所見非顛倒故，是故彼皆以宿作為因。
items.en: This arises from observing that a person's present conduct does not reliably determine their outcome. Why is this? Because they observe that some, though acting through entirely proper means, nonetheless meet with suffering, while others, though acting through improper means, nonetheless arrive at happiness. They reason thus: were present conduct truly the cause of these outcomes, this observation would have to be a distortion — yet what they observe is plainly not a distortion. Therefore, they conclude, prior deeds alone must be the true cause in every case.

items.zh: 由此理故，彼起如是見，立如是論。
items.en: On the strength of this reasoning, they hold this view and establish this doctrine.

items.title: The Refutation: If Only Past Karma Matters, Why Does Austerity Do Anything?

items.zh: 今應問彼：汝何所欲？現法方便所招之苦，為用宿作為因？為用現法方便為因？若用宿作為因者，汝先所說，由勤精進吐舊業故，現在新業由不作因之所害故，如是於後不復有漏，乃至廣說，不應道理。
items.en: One should press them thus: what, precisely, do you mean? Is the suffering brought about by present ascetic effort itself caused by prior deeds, or is it caused by that present effort? If it is caused by prior deeds, then your own earlier claim — that diligent effort purges old karma, that refraining from new action prevents its accumulation, and that freedom from contamination thereafter follows, and so on in full — makes no sense.

items.zh: 若用現法方便為因者，汝先所說，凡諸世間所有士夫補特伽羅所受，皆由宿作為因，不應道理。如是現法方便苦宿作為因故，現法士夫用為因故，皆不應道理，是故此論非如理說。
items.en: If it is caused by present effort, then your own earlier claim — that every experience of every person in the world is invariably caused by prior deeds alone — makes no sense. Thus, whether the suffering of present ascetic effort is said to be caused by prior deeds, or the present person's own effort is said to be its cause, neither makes sense — and so this doctrine is not a soundly reasoned teaching.

items.title: The Real Answer: Suffering Has Three Different Kinds of Cause

items.zh: 我今當說如實因相。或有諸苦唯用宿作為因。猶如有一，自業增上力故，生諸惡趣或貧窮家。或復有苦雜因所生。謂如有一，因邪事王，不獲樂果而反致苦。
items.en: I shall now state the true nature of cause. There is suffering caused by prior deeds alone — as when someone, through the sheer dominant force of their own past karma, is born into an unfortunate destiny or into poverty. There is also suffering produced by a mixture of causes — as when someone, serving a king through improper means, fails to obtain happy results and instead meets with suffering.

items.zh: 如事於王如是，由諸言說商賈等業、由事農業、由劫盜業、或於他有情作損害事，若有福者，獲得富樂，若無福者，雖設功用而無果遂。或復有法，純由現在功用因得。如新所造引餘有業；或聽聞正法，於法覺察；或復發起威儀業路，或復修學工巧業處；如是等類，唯因現在士夫功用。
items.en: As with serving a king, so too with a writer's craft, with trade, with farming, with theft, or with harming other beings: one who has merit obtains wealth and happiness even through improper means, while one without merit finds no result despite great effort — such results are a mixture of past merit and present method. And there is, further, that which is obtained purely through present effort: newly performed karma that draws a further rebirth; hearing the true Dharma and awakening insight into it; the arising of one's own bodily conduct and bearing; or learning a craft or trade — all such things depend solely on the present person's own effort.

items.title: The Seventh Doctrine: A Sovereign Creator Behind Everything

items.zh: 自在等作者論者，由如有一，或沙門、或婆羅門，起如是見，立如是論：凡諸世間所有士夫補特伽羅所受，彼一切或以自在變化為因，或餘丈夫變化為因，諸如是等。謂說自在等不平等因論者作如是計。
items.en: The doctrine of a sovereign lord as maker: there are certain renunciants or brahmins who hold such a view and establish such a doctrine — that whatever any person in the world experiences is caused, in every case, either by the transformative power of a sovereign lord, or by the transformative power of some other person (puruṣa), and so on. It is those who propound this doctrine of an unequal cause who hold this position.

items.zh: 問：何因緣故，起如是見，立如是論？答：由教及理。教如前說。理者，猶如有一，為性尋思，為性觀察，廣說如前。
items.en: Question: For what reason do they hold this view and establish this doctrine? Answer: Because of scripture and reasoning. Scripture is as explained before. Reasoning means that someone is a speculator by nature and an examiner by nature, as explained at length before.

items.zh: 彼由現見於因果中，世間有情不隨欲轉，故作此計。所以者何？現見世間有情，於彼因時欲修淨業，不遂本欲，反更為惡。於彼果時，願生善趣樂世界中，不遂本欲，墮惡趣等。意謂受樂，不遂所欲，反受諸苦。
items.en: They arrive at this by observing that beings in the world, with respect to cause and effect, cannot make things turn out as they wish. Why is this? Because they observe beings who, at the time of acting, wish to perform wholesome deeds yet fail to realise that wish and instead do wrong; and who, at the time of receiving results, wish to be reborn into a fortunate, happy world yet fail to realise that wish and instead fall into an unfortunate destiny. They wish for happiness, and, failing to obtain what they wish, instead experience suffering.

items.zh: 由見此故，彼作是思：世間諸物必應別有作者、生者，及變化者為彼物父，謂自在天，或復其餘。
items.en: Seeing this, they reason: everything in the world must therefore have some further maker, producer, and transformer standing behind it as its father — namely, a sovereign lord, or some other such being.

blocks.text: Fascicle 7 completes the sixteen mistaken doctrines. Today: the sixth, that everything we experience comes from past deeds alone, and the beginning of the seventh, that a sovereign creator causes everything. Both still have followers today, and both are views a Buddhist can slip into: treating karma as fate, or treating the Buddha or a deity as one who arranges our lives.

Several formal questions are missing from Ru-Yi's translation (now supplied in our own translation, marked as ours) ("Why do they hold this view? Through scripture and reasoning …", 0308c26, 0309a05, 0309b01).

The sixth doctrine is held by the **Nirgrantha** (無繫) ascetics, the Jains. Venerable Miào Jìng: 繫 here means clothing; they went naked, and so were also called "the shameless ones". They hold that all present suffering comes from past wrongdoing and can be purged by austerity, after which "no further contamination arises". Master Cháng Bǎi describes their practices: standing on one leg "like a golden rooster", lying on scorching ground in the sun.

Present conduct does not reliably determine outcomes: "some, though acting through entirely proper means, nonetheless meet with suffering, while others, though acting through improper means, nonetheless prosper." So, they conclude, everything must come from the past.

Venerable Miào Jìng warns that a version of this lives among Buddhists: "Some among us monastics teach that suffering more erases wrongdoing; here we can see that deliberately making yourself suffer doesn't erase it."

A dilemma: is the suffering of austerity itself caused by past deeds, or by present effort? If by past deeds, austerity cannot purge them, since it is just more of their result. If by present effort, then not everything comes from past deeds. Master Cháng Bǎi's image for how karma is really ended: "If there's rubbish there and you don't make the effort to sweep it out, it can't clear itself." Afflictions are cut by calm and insight, not burned away by pain.

The treatise's own view is balanced. Some suffering comes from past deeds alone, such as birth in an unfortunate realm or into poverty. Some comes from a mixture, as when one serves a king and the meritorious prosper while others toil in vain. Some comes from present effort alone, as from heavy labour. Karma is real, but it is not fate; present action also counts. This matters for practice: it is the reason effort is worthwhile.

The seventh doctrine: "Whatever any person in the world experiences is caused, in every case, either by the transformative power of a sovereign lord (自在, *Īśvara*) or by that of some other great being." Venerable Miào Jìng, citing Kuījī, explains "great being" (丈夫) as the clung-to real self or spirit of Sāṃkhya and Vaiśeṣika. Master Cháng Bǎi, citing the *Cheng Weishi Lun*, says "and the like" includes Maheśvara, Brahmā, time, direction, nature, space, and the self: anything posited as a single cause of all.

The treatise calls them "propounders of an unequal cause". Venerable Miào Jìng: "What is the lord's cause? The lord exists without cause; that is unequal. Buddhism is equal: all dharmas arise from conditions; not a single one is an exception."

They observe that beings cannot make cause and effect follow their wishes: wanting good, they do wrong; wanting a good rebirth, they fall; wanting pleasure, they suffer. So something else must be in charge. The Buddhist answer, given tomorrow, is that what is "in charge" is our own past karma and present conditions, not another being's will.

quiz.q: According to the treatise, who holds the doctrine of prior deeds as cause?
quiz.why: "It is the Nirgrantha ascetics — the unclothed renunciants — who hold this position." They hold all present suffering comes from past wrongdoing and must be purged "through extreme self-mortification practised in this very life." B held effect-in-cause in fascicle 6.

quiz.q: According to the treatise, why do the Nirgranthas hold that prior deeds alone are the cause?
options: present conduct doesn't reliably determine outcomes — some act rightly yet suffer, some act wrongly yet prosper
quiz.why: "They observe that some, though acting through entirely proper means, nonetheless meet with suffering, while others, though acting through improper means, nonetheless arrive at happiness." Master Cháng Bǎi: e.g., honest business that earns nothing; "without careful reflection, most people fall into this thinking too."

quiz.q: How does the treatise refute the doctrine with a dilemma?
options: is the suffering of austerity caused by prior deeds or present effort? If prior, austerity can't purge karma; if present, "all is prior deeds" fails
quiz.why: "Is the suffering brought about by present ascetic effort itself caused by prior deeds, or is it caused by that present effort?" Either answer contradicts their own claims. Master Cháng Bǎi: "Austerity itself brings suffering, and without calm and insight one can't stop making karma."

quiz.q: According to the treatise's own account, what three kinds of cause does suffering have?
options: prior deeds alone (birth in a bad destiny or poverty); mixed causes (serving a king wrongly — the meritorious prosper, others toil in vain); present effort alone (hearing Dharma, learning a craft)
quiz.why: "There is suffering caused by prior deeds alone … There is also suffering produced by a mixture of causes … And there is, further, that which is obtained purely through present effort." Venerable Miào Jìng: one with much past merit won't suffer even serving a king improperly — that's the mixed case.

quiz.q: According to the treatise, what does the doctrine of a sovereign maker claim?
options: all that people experience is caused by the transformative power of a sovereign lord or some other great being
quiz.why: "Whatever any person in the world experiences is caused, in every case, either by the transformative power of a sovereign lord, or by the transformative power of some other great being." A is Buddhism; B fascicle 6's atomists; D the eleventh doctrine.

quiz.q: The text calls them "propounders of an unequal cause." Why "unequal," according to Venerable Miào Jìng?
options: everything has the lord as cause while the lord has no cause — that's unequal; Buddhism says all dharmas arise from conditions, without exception
quiz.why: Venerable Miào Jìng: "But what is the lord's cause? The lord exists without cause — that is unequal"; "Buddhism is equal: all dharmas arise from conditions; not a single dharma doesn't."

quiz.q: According to the treatise, what leads them to posit a sovereign maker?
options: seeing that beings can't make cause and effect follow their wishes — wanting good, they do wrong; wanting a good rebirth, they fall; wanting pleasure, they suffer
quiz.why: "They arrive at this by observing that beings in the world, with respect to cause and effect, cannot make things turn out as they wish." Master Cháng Bǎi: "Say one studies hard for university but fails; works hard for money but can't earn it." So they infer a maker standing as "father" over things.
